content.tldr: Encryption is a two-way mathematical operation intended for confidentiality that can be reversed using a key, while hashing is a one-way operation intended for integrity that cannot be reversed.
content.simple_explanation: Encryption takes plaintext and converts it into ciphertext using an encryption key; anyone possessing the corresponding decryption key can recover the original data. In contrast, a hash function takes an arbitrary-length message and computes a fixed-length digest through irreversible mathematical compression. Hashing verifies data integrity (confirming a file was not altered in transit) and stores password verifiers without exposing credentials.
content.real_world_example: Cooking: chopping and baking apples into an applesauce puree is a hash (one-way; you cannot turn applesauce back into fresh whole apples); placing an apple inside a locked safe is encryption (reversible when unlocked with the combination).
content.why_it_matters_and_pitfalls: Storing user passwords using reversible encryption is a dangerous anti-pattern: if the decryption key is compromised, every user password in the organization is instantly leaked in plaintext. Passwords must always be hashed with salted, slow adaptive algorithms.
